blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
At the executive level, British indirection stops being a curiosity and becomes a strategic instrument. The senior leaders who use it best understand exactly when to deploy it — to protect a colleague's face, to buy themselves thinking time, to signal a shift in position without committing to it publicly — and when to drop it and speak with unusual directness for effect.

The real skill lies in calibration. A mild softener at the wrong moment can sound patronising; a sharp sentence at the wrong moment can sound aggressive. The senior British communicator has, over time, developed an almost musical ear for the right temperature in the room, and adjusts by half-tones rather than whole octaves.

There is also a protective function. Indirection gives everyone room to reconsider without shame. A leader who has said "I wonder if we might want to look at this again" has not committed to anything, which means the team can come back with a different view without anyone losing face. It is, in its quiet way, one of the most humane forms of leadership English offers.

items.q: According to the text, at the executive level British indirection becomes…
options: a sign of weakness under pressure
a cultural curiosity to be tolerated
items.why: "British indirection stops being a curiosity and becomes a strategic instrument."

items.q: What does the text say the "real skill" of indirection lies in?
options: Calibration — matching the tone to the moment
Memorising a set of fixed softeners
items.why: "The real skill lies in calibration" — a moderação certa para cada momento.

items.q: The image of adjusting "by half-tones rather than whole octaves" suggests that skilled leaders…
options: avoid changing their tone at all
make small, precise shifts in tone rather than dramatic ones
items.why: Inferência: a metáfora musical descreve ajustes finos e graduais, não mudanças bruscas.

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Directness is sometimes deployed deliberately for effect.
Indirection can protect a colleague's dignity.
The wrong softener can come across as patronising.
Indirection is merely a quaint national habit with no strategic value.
items.why: Inferência: a tese do texto é justamente que a indiretude deixa de ser curiosidade e vira instrumento estratégico.

items.q: The example "I wonder if we might want to look at this again" is used to show that indirection…
options: lets people change their minds without losing face
commits the leader firmly to a decision
hides a leader's true intentions from the team
items.why: "has not committed to anything… without anyone losing face" — a função protetora deixa espaço para reconsiderar.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Charlotte analisar a transcrição de uma reunião executiva. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let me walk you through this transcript, because I think it's a small masterclass. We've got a new director on the call, and the CEO uses indirection five separate times — and each one is doing a different job.

Take the opening. The director pushes a rather aggressive number, and instead of contradicting him, the CEO says, "That's an interesting figure — I wonder what assumptions sit underneath it." Notice she hasn't disagreed. She's bought herself thinking time, and she's invited him to expose the weak link himself. Beautifully economical.

Then, halfway through, something changes. There's a genuine safety concern on the table, and suddenly the softeners disappear. "No. We don't ship until that's fixed." Four words. And because she has been so measured up to that point, those four words land with real force. That's the calibration we keep talking about — she's earned her directness.

What I want you to take from this is that none of it is accidental. Every hedge, every pause, every blunt sentence is a choice. Read it that way, and you'll start to hear what people are actually signalling.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: How many times does the CEO use indirection in the transcript Charlotte analyses?
items.why: "the CEO uses indirection five separate times — and each one is doing a different job."

items.q: When the director pushes an aggressive number, the CEO's response mainly serves to…
options: publicly reject the figure at once
buy thinking time and let him expose the weak assumption himself
hand the decision to someone else
items.why: "She's bought herself thinking time, and she's invited him to expose the weak link himself."

items.q: Why does Charlotte say the CEO's four blunt words "land with real force"?
options: Because the director had already agreed
Because she had been so measured up to that point
Because she repeated them several times
items.why: "because she has been so measured up to that point, those four words land with real force."

items.q: What does Charlotte imply by calling the transcript "a small masterclass"?
options: The CEO's use of language was skilful and worth studying
The transcript was hard to follow
items.why: Inferência: "masterclass" indica que Charlotte vê o desempenho como exemplar e didático.

items.q: What is the main lesson Charlotte wants the listener to draw?
options: That directness should always be avoided in meetings
That new directors talk too much
That every hedge, pause and blunt sentence is a deliberate choice
items.why: Inferência: "none of it is accidental… Every hedge, every pause, every blunt sentence is a choice."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "She knew exactly when to deploy a softener and when to drop it." To deploy here means to…
options: put to use for a purpose
items.why: Deploy = empregar, colocar em uso de forma deliberada.

items.q: "A softener offered too soon can come across as patronising." Patronising means…
options: condescending, as if talking down to someone
items.why: Patronising = condescendente, tratar o outro como inferior.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "The best communicators ___ their tone to the room, adjusting by tiny degrees."
items.why: Calibrate = calibrar, ajustar com precisão ao contexto.

items.q: "He raised the objection with real ___ , giving the junior analyst room to retreat with dignity." Choose the word that fits.
items.why: Indirection = indiretude, que aqui protege a face do outro.

items.q: "It is, in its quiet way, one of the most humane forms of leadership." Humane means…
items.why: Humane = humano, compassivo — que preserva a dignidade das pessoas.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem em reuniões executivas. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The board still has to sign off on the revised figure." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Two directors quietly pushed back on the timeline." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, contestar — sem necessariamente recusar de vez.

items.q: "She softened the message, then let the point land before continuing." Here, to land means to…
items.why: Land (para uma frase/mensagem) = surtir o efeito pretendido, calar fundo.

items.q: "He agreed to the plan in the room but never followed through." He…
options: failed to carry it through to the end
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado — aqui, o que ele não fez.

items.q: "A single blunt sentence, well timed, can move the needle more than an hour of hedging." This means it can…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, provocar uma diferença perceptível.
